item.title: Identification, estimation, and robust inference of structural autoregressions for multidimensional data
item.description: arXiv:2611.13169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many modern datasets such as cross-country panels have a multidimensional structure. Conventional approaches on structural vector autoregressions for identifying structural shocks are not directly suited to these settings where data are naturally organized as matrices or tensors, since the number of parameters grows rapidly and identifying restrictions become hard to impose. We introduce a class of structural autoregressions for multidimensional data that achieves tractability and global identification by assuming a Kronecker structure on the model coefficients. We develop a minimum-distance estimator and establish its asymptotic distribution. To accommodate approximate Kronecker separability, we develop confidence intervals for the structural impulse response functions that are robust to local misspecification, and we show their asymptotic validity. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate the validity of the asymptotic approximations and good finite-sample performance of the estimator and their (robust) confidence intervals. We illustrate the methods on a country panel dataset to analyze the dynamic and spillover effects of US monetary policy shocks.
item.dc:creator: Bernhard van der Sluis

item.title: Instrumental variables with treatment clusters
item.description: arXiv:2611.13313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many policy evaluations include multiple unordered treatments. A common approach is to aggregate these treatments into clusters and apply instrumental variable (IV) methods at the treatment cluster level: The clusters are treated as binary treatments and the IV assumptions are invoked at the cluster level. This paper shows that IV with treatment clusters identifies a weighted average of local average treatment effects (LATEs) under a set of assumptions at the unclustered treatment level. When data on unclustered treatment choice is available, we propose testable necessary conditions for the causal interpretation of IV with treatment clusters. We illustrate our methods with empirical applications to the causal effects of fields of study aggregated into STEM and non-STEM clusters or eight broad study directions.
item.dc:creator: Didier Nibbering, Matthijs Oosterveen, Pedro Luis Silva

item.title: Backtesting High-Dimensional Expected Shortfall
item.description: arXiv:2611.13882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forecast evaluation increasingly uses high-dimensional predictors, but estimation and regularization of large predictive models can distort conventional backtests. This issue is particularly important for forecasting downside risk, where the signal-to-noise ratio is low. We develop out-of-sample Expected Shortfall (ES) backtests that remove the large first-order bias effects of estimating high-dimensional Value-at-Risk, ES, and the evaluation instrument. In a linear ES specification, the proposed methods are easily implemented as Double Lasso with a tail-size-adjusted score as a generated dependent variable. More generally, we characterize orthogonal ES backtesting moments, and establish oracle equivalence and valid inference under time-series dependence and repeated estimation with overlapping and expanding training windows. Simulations show that conventional backtests can severely overreject ES optimal forecasts, whereas orthogonalization improves size control. An application to downside-growth forecasting for G7 economies finds evidence against a US growth-only ES specification, even though forecast-oriented regularization selects no additional financial predictors. The application also shows that accounting for estimation can change rejection decisions in either direction. These findings highlight the distinct roles of predictive variable selection and backtesting in the evaluation of high-dimensional tail-risk models.
item.dc:creator: Zaichao Du, Juan Carlos Escanciano, Pei Pei

item.title: Semiparametric Inference in Panel Data with Interactive and High-dimensional Confounding
item.description: arXiv:2611.14385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops inference for a low-dimensional treatment coefficient in partially linear panel models with high-dimensional observed covariates and latent interactive confounding. Flexible adjustment for observed covariates can leave correlated factor components in treatment and outcome residuals, invalidating standard double/debiased machine learning (DML). We propose Factor-Augmented DML (FA-DML), which estimates treatment-side and reduced-form factor spaces from first-stage residuals. The estimator combines a feasible double projection with three-fold, unit-level cross-fitting. The double projection controls interactions between the two estimated factor spaces. The separate folds eliminate same-training-unit pairings in the leading disturbance components of the factor-estimation errors. Under fixed factor ranks, pervasive factor signals, strict exogeneity, and joint asymptotics in the number of units N and periods T , FA-DML is first-order equivalent to an infeasible oracle, is asymptotically normal, and admits consistent variance estimation. In the baseline simulation design with strong interactive confounding, FA-DML confidence intervals have coverage close to the nominal level. Standard DML and a two-fold variant that estimates both factor spaces on the same units substantially undercover. In an application to U.S. states, FA-DML finds that a 10% increase in the real minimum wage is associated with a roughly 1.1% lower 50/10 wage ratio. The estimate is stable across control sets and first-stage learners.
item.dc:creator: Bin Chen, Yukun Ma, Qiyang Yu

item.title: Hedging out the HEDGE Bias: Identifying Dynamic Partial-Equilibrium Effects with Panel LP-IV
item.description: arXiv:2611.14434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-sectional designs are widely used to estimate dynamic partial-equilibrium effects of an aggregate treatment. We show analytically that these estimates are biased when exposures to the treatment and to aggregate confounders are correlated or the confounders feed back into the treatment. This paper develops the heterogeneous-exposure local-projection instrumental variables (HELP-IV) framework, which compares units while holding the confounder path fixed by instrumenting the treatment and this path with exposure-weighted shock proxies. We prove that HELP-IV identifies the partial-equilibrium effect. We further extend the framework, with the corresponding inference, to multiple exposure margins and confounders, forward-looking outcomes, and cumulative multipliers. Finally, we apply HELP-IV to state fiscal multipliers and regional stock-wealth effects, where it yields partial-equilibrium effects that are smaller than conventional estimates and deliver different implications when ported to macroeconomic models.
item.dc:creator: Endong Wang, Ren Zhang

item.title: Prediction Inference for Hybrid Models on Realized Volatility Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.13212v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GARCH-LSTM hybrid models have become increasingly popular in the volatility forecasting literature. To date, these models have almost exclusively focused on point estimation and accuracy measures such as RMSE and MAPE, while failing to assess the uncertainty of these point estimates. We approach this gap in two ways. First, we extend the existing GARCH-LSTM model by modeling the conditional mean with an ARMA structure. Second, we develop a forward bootstrap algorithm to build multi-step-ahead prediction intervals for future realized volatility. In order to address the notorious undercoverage of prediction intervals, we implement two solutions. One draws bootstrap innovations from the empirical residual distribution to mimic the fat-tail property of financial series. The other utilizes principles from conformal prediction to systematically extend the prediction interval length. We evaluate the methods in simulations with heavy-tailed and time-varying GARCH processes and in rolling-window forecasts of four U.S. stock indices from 2020 to 2025. The ARMA-based hybrid gives the lowest point-forecast errors in most settings, and combining both remedies with the mean-based hybrid yields intervals closest to the nominal level among competing methods.
item.dc:creator: Kyle Parrella, Kejin Wu

item.title: Simple Estimation of Semiparametric Models with Measurement Errors
item.description: arXiv:2306.14311v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a practical way of addressing the Errors-In-Variables (EIV) problem in the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) framework. We focus on the settings in which the variability of the EIV is a fraction of that of the mismeasured variables, which is typical for empirical applications. For any initial set of moment conditions our approach provides a ``corrected'' set of moment conditions that are robust to the EIV. We show that the GMM estimator based on these moments is root-n-consistent, with the standard tests and confidence intervals providing valid inference. This is true even when the EIV are so large that naive estimators (that ignore the EIV problem) are heavily biased with their confidence intervals having 0% coverage. Our approach involves no nonparametric estimation, which is especially important for applications with many covariates and settings with multivariate EIV. In particular, the approach makes it easy to use instrumental variables to address EIV in nonlinear models.
item.dc:creator: Kirill S. Evdokimov, Andrei Zeleneev

item.title: Local Projections Inference with High-Dimensional Covariates without Exact Sparsity
item.description: arXiv:2402.07743v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a high-dimensional local projections framework for estimating impulse responses in the presence of many potential controls. Other approaches often rely on exact sparsity assumptions, but empirical macroeconomic applications may involve nuisance relationships better described by structured coefficient decay. Building on the orthogonal greedy algorithm with high-dimensional AIC (OGA+HDAIC), I propose a double-selection procedure that separately addresses the shock equation and the outcome equation within local projections. The method allows for nonexact sparsity through polynomially decaying nuisance coefficients, with rates indexed by the decay exponent rather than by an effective sparsity level. Under suitable moment, dependence, and approximation conditions, the estimator achieves asymptotic normality with HAC standard errors. Simulation evidence shows reliable coverage under shock contamination and lower point-estimation error under predictable high-dimensional outcome nuisance. I illustrate the method's practical feasibility in a monetary policy application using the FRED-MD dataset.
item.dc:creator: Jooyoung Cha

item.title: Identification in Auctions with Truncated Transaction Prices
item.description: arXiv:2510.04464v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies nonparametric identification in auction models with truncated transaction price data arising from either binding reserve prices or endogenous entry. I characterize identification under alternative information structures that differ according to whether the number of potential bidders is fixed or varies across auctions and whether the econometrician observes the number of potential or active bidders. A central insight is that identification hinges on recovering the screening threshold that determines bidder participation. The analysis provides a unified characterization of identification in first- and second-price auctions under both truncation mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Tonghui Qi

item.title: Testing Exclusion and Shape Restrictions in Potential Outcomes Models
item.description: arXiv:2512.20851v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Exclusion and shape restrictions play a central role in defining causal effects and interpreting estimates in potential outcomes models. To date, the testable implications of such restrictions have been studied on a case-by-case basis in a limited set of models. In this paper, we develop a general framework for characterizing sharp testable implications of general support restrictions on the potential response functions, based on a novel graph-based representation of the model. The framework provides a unified and constructive method for deriving all observable implications of the modeling assumptions. We illustrate the approach in several popular settings, including instrumental variables, treatment selection, mediation, and interference. As an empirical application, we revisit the US Lung Health Study and test for the presence of spillovers between spouses, specification of exposure maps, and persistence of treatment effects over time.
item.dc:creator: Hiroaki Kaido, Kirill Ponomarev

item.title: State-Dependent Local Projections and Vector Autoregressions
item.description: arXiv:2601.01622v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the relationship between state-dependent local projections (LPs) and vector autoregressions (VARs). I show nonparametrically that state-dependent LPs estimate the projection of a convex weighted average of causal effects on the state, including continuous and multidimensional states. In contrast, conventional state-dependent VARs need not have a causal interpretation, even when they model state transitions correctly. A new backshifted VAR, conditioning every prediction step on the pre-shock state, asymptotically matches the LP estimand up to its lag order.
item.dc:creator: Valentin Winkler

item.title: Exact Inference in Fixed-Effect Regressions with Concentrated Identifying Variation
item.description: arXiv:2608.04839v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In fixed-effect regressions with many groups, a handful of observations can carry most of the identifying variation left after fixed effects are removed. Conventional $t$-tests can then reject a true null more than half the time. This paper specializes the exact $t$-test of Pouliot to such designs. Contrasts chosen from the design eliminate the nuisance coefficients exactly; sign flips give finite-sample valid tests under independent symmetric errors, or compatible independent symmetric error blocks, allowing arbitrary heteroskedasticity. In two-way designs, the annihilating space is the cycle space of the bipartite observation graph and contains all within variation. This makes the choice of contrasts a graph problem. The observable capture ratio $\kappa_{\mathcal C}\in[0,1]$ measures retained identifying variation and, under diffuse homoskedastic conditions, gives the efficiency relative to an oracle test. Structured packing trades capture against the number and balance of usable signs. The matched-weight test is also asymptotically valid without symmetry when independent centered contrast scores satisfy a fourth-moment negligibility condition. In the Grunfeld investment regression, where one observation carries $73.9\%$ of the realized squared score, 32 contrasts capture $\kappa_{\mathcal C}=0.627$ and give a symmetry-based exact $95\%$ confidence interval of $[0.150, 0.450]$.
item.dc:creator: Stanis{\l}aw M. S. Halkiewicz

item.title: Where Has the Foreign Signal Gone? Contributor Composition and the Reliability of Social Media Sentiment
item.description: arXiv:2610.28175v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Social media sentiment is increasingly used to predict stock returns. Its reliability depends on the composition of the crowd generating the feed. For foreign firms, the home-market investors who know them best are underrepresented on English-language Twitter. Hence, their feed should carry a less precise signal. Reduced-form analysis of firm-level Twitter sentiment shows that sentiment noise predicts next-quarter losses less consistently for foreign stocks than for domestic stocks. The loss-on-noise slope is negative in 78 percent of quarters for domestic stocks but in only 48 percent for foreign stocks, with a significant mean difference in slopes. We interpret this difference through a noisy rational expectations model in which the feed carries a public signal produced by three types of contributors. Specialists post repeatedly with information about the firm, attention-driven contributors post once with information about the firm and a transient fad, and automated accounts post repeatedly with no information about the firm. The share of each contributor type and the size of the fad determine the precision of the signal, which, in turn, determines how much of the feed's noise reaches prices. The model gives repeat-author share, fad and precision from the vendor's aggregate metrics, without account-level data, whereas prior work backs out precision from price informativeness. The structural estimates show that feeds for foreign stocks have a higher share of repeat authors, a larger fad component and a less precise signal. Thus, the foreign signal did not disappear but got diluted.
item.dc:creator: Piyush Akimitsu Ulrich Hounyo

item.title: Accuracy of Uniform Inference on Fine Grid Points
item.description: arXiv:2512.18627v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Uniform confidence bands are widely used to quantify uncertainty about unknown functions in nonparametric inference. Although various methods, including the multiplier bootstrap, have been developed and theoretically justified, practical implementations typically replace the supremum over a continuum by the maximum over a finite evaluation grid. This paper investigates how this discretization affects coverage accuracy and how fine the evaluation grid must be to ensure valid uniform inference. We first illustrate through simulations of a kernel-based nonparametric estimator that coarse grids can substantially reduce uniform coverage. Surprisingly, increasing the sample size can worsen coverage on a fixed coarse grid, even as the remaining approximation error on the grid decreases. We then derive general upper bounds on the coverage probability and coverage error of uniform confidence bands based on finite-grid multiplier-bootstrap critical values, separating discretization error from the remaining approximation errors. In particular, the general coverage error bound identifies the constant in the discretization term explicitly. For local empirical processes arising from kernel smoothing, we establish primitive conditions under which coverage converges to zero even when the number of grid points diverges, and conditions ensuring asymptotically nominal coverage. We further develop two implementable grid selection rules for a user-chosen discretization tolerance. Gaussian Monte Carlo experiments show that the proposed rules select grid sizes close to those required by the Monte Carlo benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Shunsuke Imai

item.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.09792v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.
item.dc:creator: Ayush Sawarni, Wenqian Xing, Tijana Zrnic, Ramesh Johari, Vasilis Syrgkanis
